style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: AAN Practice Guidelines & EAN Guidelines on Neurological Disorders (2024)

clinical_targets.goal: ≥ 50% reduction in monthly attack/seizure frequency from baseline
Preservation of modified Rankin Scale score ≤ 2
Maintenance of baseline MoCA / MMSE cognitive scores

Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Dizziness and Vertigo focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Dizziness and Vertigo require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Dizziness and Vertigo.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Gabapentinoids, levetiracetam, and topiramate require strict renal dose adjustments.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Valproate, carbamazepine, and phenytoin are extensively metabolized by the liver; monitor serum levels.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Valproate is strictly contraindicated due to high neural tube and neurodevelopmental teratogenicity.
special_populations.elderly: Increased sensitivity to CNS sedatives, anticholinergics, and antiepileptic neurotoxicity; start low and titrate slowly.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is dizziness and vertigo? Dizziness and vertigo are not the same thing, but they are often mixed up. Dizziness can make you feel lightheaded, woozy or unsteady on your feet. Vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning even when nothing is moving. These feelings may get worse when you walk, stand up, or move your head, and they can make you lose your balance . You may also have nausea, vomiting , sweating , trouble walking, or ringing in your ears . What causes dizziness and vertigo? Dizziness and vertigo can happen to anyone, but they are more common as you get older. As people age, they may have more health conditions and take more medicines, which increases the chance of dizziness. Common causes of dizziness and vertigo may include: A sudden drop in blood pressure Dehydration Getting up too quickly Certain medicines Inner ear problems , such as Meniere's disease , or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), the most common cause of vertigo Motion sickness Migraines A head injury or ear surgery Sometimes dizziness or vertigo is a symptom of another condition. How is the cause of dizziness and vertigo diagnosed? Your provider will ask about your medicines and symptoms and may do a physical exam. They may check your hearing, balance, and how you walk. You may need an imaging test if your provider thinks you may have had a stroke or if you've had a head injury. What are the treatments for dizziness and vertigo? Dizziness often gets better on its own, but if it keeps happening, your provider can help you find the cause and the right treatment. Treatment depends on the cause and may include balance exercises and medicines. Get emergency help right away if you have sudden or severe dizziness or vertigo along with vision problems, slurred speech or weakness. These may be signs of a more serious condition. NIH: National Institutes of Health
style_3_monograph.treatment: Your provider may perform a procedure called the Epley maneuver . It is a series of head movements to reposition the canaliths in your inner ear. The procedure may need to be repeated if symptoms come back, but this treatment works best to cure BPPV. Your provider may refer you to vestibular rehabilitation or teach you other repositioning exercises that you can do at home, but may take longer than the Epley maneuver to work. Other exercises, such as balance therapy, may help some people. Some medicines can help relieve spinning sensations: Antihistamines Anticholinergics Sedative-hypnotics But, these medicines often do not work well for treating vertigo. Follow instructions on how to take care for yourself at home . To keep your symptoms from getting worse, avoid the positions that trigger it.
